name: Idaho
answer: Idaho fly fishing is western freestone and spring creek water, with rainbow, cutthroat and brown trout as the mainstays. The Henry's Fork, Silver Creek and the South Fork of the Snake are the headline rivers. A license is required from age 14; the season runs year-round on many waters, with the best dry-fly fishing from June through September.
summary: Rainbow, cutthroat and brown trout on spring creeks and freestone rivers. Technical dry-fly water on the Henry's Fork, salmonflies on the South Fork.
whatMakesItDifferent: Idaho packs two very different kinds of trout water into one state. The Henry's Fork of the Snake and Silver Creek are flat, weed-rich spring creeks where fish get an unhurried look at the fly and refusals are the norm — this is some of the most technical dry-fly water in North America. An hour or two away, the South Fork of the Snake and the Salmon are big, pushy freestone rivers where a size 6 salmonfly gets eaten without much argument. Very few states ask an angler to fish both ends of that spectrum in the same week.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Widespread; the Henry's Fork rainbows are famously selective.

species.name: Yellowstone cutthroat
species.note: Native. The South Fork of the Snake holds one of the strongest remaining populations.

species.name: Westslope cutthroat
species.note: Native to the north — the St. Joe and Kelly Creek are the classic waters.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Silver Creek and the Big Wood, and the lower Henry's Fork.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: High-country streams and lakes.

species.name: Bull trout
species.note: Native char, ESA-listed. Catch and release only, and they may not be targeted — check current rules.

species.name: Steelhead
species.note: Clearwater and Salmon river systems. Requires a separate permit.

waters.name: Henry's Fork of the Snake
waters.note: The Railroad Ranch section is flat, slow and famously difficult. Green Drakes in June, then PMDs and Tricos into autumn.

waters.name: Silver Creek
waters.note: A spring creek near Picabo, long associated with Ernest Hemingway, who lived and is buried in nearby Ketchum. Gin-clear, weedy, and unforgiving of drag.

waters.name: South Fork of the Snake
waters.note: Big freestone water below Palisades. Salmonflies in early summer, cutthroat on dry flies all season.

waters.name: Big Wood River
waters.note: Freestone through Ketchum and Hailey. Accessible, and it fishes well in autumn.

waters.name: St. Joe River
waters.note: Northern Idaho, native westslope cutthroat, and a long catch-and-release stretch.

waters.name: Kelly Creek
waters.note: Remote northern cutthroat water; a long drive and worth it.

seasons.what: Runoff on freestone rivers. Fish tailwaters and spring creeks; Baetis on gray days.
Salmonflies on the South Fork and Henry's Fork. Green Drakes on the Henry's Fork — the busiest weeks of the year.
PMDs, Tricos in the mornings, terrestrials on the banks. Dawn and dusk in the heat.
Mahogany duns, Baetis, aggressive pre-spawn browns. Many anglers' favorite month.
Midges on tailwaters and spring creeks. Silver Creek and the lower Henry's Fork stay fishable.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 14. Non-residents can buy annual or daily licenses.
Bull trout are ESA-listed: catch and release only, and they may not be targeted. Learn to identify them before fishing northern and central Idaho.
A separate Salmon & Steelhead permit is required to target steelhead or chinook.
Some waters are catch-and-release or artificial-lure-only. Rules vary water by water and change annually.

license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026 published rates for an adult annual fishing license and exclude processing fees and the depredation/access fee. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

localNote: The Reel Deal Deck is made in Eagle, Idaho, so this is our home water.

name: Pennsylvania
answer: Pennsylvania fly fishing means limestone spring creeks and freestone mountain streams, with wild brown and brook trout alongside a very large stocking program. Penns Creek, Spring Creek and the Letort are the classic waters. You need both a fishing license and a separate trout permit, and stocked waters close ahead of the spring opening day.
summary: Limestone spring creeks and wild brook trout, plus one of the largest trout stocking programs in the country. Technical water with a long angling history.
whatMakesItDifferent: Pennsylvania's limestone spring creeks are the reason American technical dry-fly fishing exists as a discipline. Water filtering through limestone emerges at a near-constant temperature, rich in the minerals that grow weed, insects and heavy trout — and it stays fishable in January and in August when a freestone stream nearby will not. The Letort Spring Run in Carlisle is where Vince Marinaro and Charlie Fox worked out much of the modern terrestrial and technical dry-fly canon in the mid-twentieth century. Fish that live in slow, clear, weed-rich water get a very long look at a fly, which is why Pennsylvania anglers tend to fish finer tippet and smaller flies than the national average.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: The state fish and the only native trout. Wild populations in mountain freestone streams.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and self-sustaining in the limestone creeks; the main quarry on Penns and Spring Creek.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Mostly stocked, though some streams hold holdover fish.

waters.name: Penns Creek
waters.note: Best known for its Green Drake hatch in late May and early June, which draws anglers from across the country.

waters.name: Spring Creek
waters.note: Near State College. All wild trout, catch-and-release, and fishable year-round.

waters.name: Letort Spring Run
waters.note: Small, slow, weedy and very difficult. Historically important out of proportion to its size.

waters.name: Yellow Breeches Creek
waters.note: Limestone water at Boiling Springs with a well-known year-round section.

waters.name: Little Juniata River
waters.note: Limestone-influenced freestone; strong Sulphur and caddis hatches.

waters.name: Upper Delaware River
waters.note: On the New York border. Big water, wild fish, and genuinely hard.

seasons.what: Stocked trout waters are open. Midges and small nymphs on the limestone creeks.
Stocked trout waters close ahead of opening day. Wild trout and year-round sections remain open.
Opening day, then Grannom caddis, Hendricksons and Sulphurs. The busiest stretch of the season.
The Green Drake hatch on Penns Creek. Sulphurs continue; evenings are the thing.
Tricos in the morning, terrestrials through the day. Limestone creeks hold up when freestone streams get too warm.
Baetis, cooler water, and stocked waters reopen the day after Labor Day.

regulations: You need a fishing license AND a separate Trout Permit to fish for trout in stocked, regulated or designated trout waters.
Stocked trout waters are closed from 16 February until 8am on opening day (4 April in 2026), apart from designated year-round sections and Mentored Youth Day.
Stocked waters reopen the day after Labor Day and run to 31 December.
Class A wild trout streams, delayed-harvest and artificial-lures-only sections all carry their own rules. Check the water before you fish it.

license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026 published rates for an adult annual fishing license. A Trout Permit ($14.97 in 2026) is required in addition, for any trout water. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Montana
answer: Montana fly fishing is big freestone and tailwater river fishing, with rainbow, brown and cutthroat trout as the mainstays and native Arctic grayling in a few drainages. The Madison, Yellowstone, Missouri and Big Hole are the headline rivers. A license is required from age 12, and a Conservation License and AIS Prevention Pass must be bought alongside it. Late June through September is the heart of the season.
summary: Big freestone rivers and famous tailwaters: the Madison, Yellowstone, Missouri and Big Hole. Salmonflies in June, hoppers in August, open stream access.
whatMakesItDifferent: Montana's Stream Access Law is the thing that sets it apart. Anglers may wade and fish any river or stream below the ordinary high-water mark regardless of who owns the bank, so long as they get in at a bridge, public road or public land. In most of the West a famous river means a famous private ranch; in Montana it means miles of water you can legally stand in. The second difference is scale — the Madison runs as a fifty-mile riffle below Quake Lake, the Yellowstone is the longest undammed river in the lower 48, and the Missouri below Holter is a weed-rich tailwater holding thousands of trout per mile. The flip side is heat: in a dry August, Fish, Wildlife & Parks imposes Hoot Owl restrictions that close rivers in the afternoon, so a Montana trip plans around mornings.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Wild and self-sustaining on the Madison, Missouri and Bighorn.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Strongest on the Missouri, Beaverhead and Bighorn; aggressive and territorial in autumn.

species.name: Yellowstone cutthroat
species.note: Native to the Yellowstone drainage and the upper river.

species.name: Westslope cutthroat
species.note: Native west of the Continental Divide — the Blackfoot and upper Clark Fork tributaries.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Small streams, beaver ponds and spring creeks.

species.name: Bull trout
species.note: Native char, ESA-listed. They may not be targeted on most waters — learn to identify them.

species.name: Arctic grayling
species.note: The Big Hole holds one of the last native river-dwelling populations in the lower 48.

species.name: Mountain whitefish
species.note: Native, abundant, and perfectly willing to take a dry fly.

waters.name: Madison River
waters.note: The fifty-mile riffle below Quake Lake. Wade-friendly, crowded in July, and the salmonfly hatch is worth the company.

waters.name: Yellowstone River
waters.note: The longest undammed river in the lower 48. Mother's Day caddis before runoff, then cutthroat on dries all summer.

waters.name: Missouri River below Holter Dam
waters.note: A tailwater at Craig. Weed-rich, heavy fish, PMDs and Tricos, and Baetis into November.

waters.name: Big Hole River
waters.note: Salmonflies in June, and the only river in the lower 48 with a native fluvial grayling population.

waters.name: Bighorn River
waters.note: Tailwater below Afterbay. Extraordinary trout numbers, with sow bugs and midges that work all year.

waters.name: Rock Creek
waters.note: Near Missoula. Accessible, generous, and a good first Montana river.

seasons.what: Skwala stoneflies on the Bitterroot and lower Clark Fork. Midges and Baetis on the tailwaters.
Mother's Day caddis on the Yellowstone, then runoff. The tailwaters carry the month.
Salmonflies on the Big Hole, Rock Creek and the Madison, with golden stones and PMDs behind them.
Hoppers, ants and spruce moths. Watch for Hoot Owl restrictions and fish the mornings.
Baetis and pre-spawn browns in October, then midges on the Missouri and Bighorn through winter.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 12. A Conservation License and an Angler AIS Prevention Pass must be purchased alongside it before it is valid.
The Stream Access Law allows public use of rivers and streams below the ordinary high-water mark, but you must enter at a bridge, public road or public land — not across private ground.
Hoot Owl restrictions close some rivers from 2pm to midnight when water runs too warm. They are announced in-season by FWP.
Yellowstone National Park issues its own permit. A Montana license is not valid inside the park.
Bull trout are ESA-listed and may not be targeted on most waters. Rules vary river by river and change annually.

license.priceNote: Montana sells fishing in parts. The resident total is an $8 Conservation License, a $21 season fishing license and a $2 Angler AIS Prevention Pass; the non-resident total is $10, $100 and $7.50. The license year runs 1 March to the end of February. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Colorado
answer: Colorado fly fishing is high-altitude tailwater and mountain river fishing, with rainbow, brown and brook trout plus native cutthroat in the headwaters. The South Platte, Fryingpan, Gunnison, Arkansas and Roaring Fork are the headline waters. A license is required from age 16, anglers 18 to 64 also need a Habitat Stamp, and the tailwaters fish all twelve months.
summary: Technical tailwaters and Gold Medal water. Small flies on the South Platte, mysis-fed browns on the Fryingpan, and caddis climbing the Arkansas in May.
whatMakesItDifferent: Colorado's rivers are built on snowmelt, which means most freestone water is unfishable brown soup through May and June. The state's fly fishing therefore grew up around dam-released tailwaters that stay cold and clear every month of the year — Cheesman Canyon and the Dream Stream on the South Platte, the Fryingpan below Ruedi, the Blue below Dillon. Those stretches hold a lot of trout that see a lot of anglers and eat very small insects, and that pressure is why Colorado produced so much of the modern technical nymph canon: the RS2, Barr's Emerger and the Copper John were all tied here for exactly this water. The Fryingpan adds a quirk of its own — mysis shrimp flushed out of the reservoir grow browns to a size the river could not otherwise support. Everything also happens high: much of this is fished between 7,000 and 10,000 feet, where afternoon thunderstorms are routine and the first day is slower than you expect.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Widespread, and the main quarry on most tailwaters.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild throughout. The Fryingpan's mysis-fed browns are the famous ones.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: High-country streams, beaver ponds and alpine lakes. Small and abundant.

species.name: Cutbow
species.note: Rainbow-cutthroat hybrids, common on the South Platte.

species.name: Greenback cutthroat
species.note: The state fish. ESA-listed and restricted to a handful of restored headwater streams.

species.name: Colorado River cutthroat
species.note: Native on the Western Slope.

species.name: Rio Grande cutthroat
species.note: Native in the southern drainages.

waters.name: South Platte River
waters.note: Cheesman Canyon and the Dream Stream. Gin-clear, heavily fished, and a lesson in long tippet and small flies.

waters.name: Fryingpan River
waters.note: Tailwater below Ruedi. Mysis shrimp, outsized browns, and green drakes in July.

waters.name: Roaring Fork River
waters.note: Freestone through Basalt and Carbondale. Drakes in summer and a very strong autumn.

waters.name: Gunnison Gorge
waters.note: A hike-in canyon below the Black Canyon. Stoneflies, big water, and far fewer people.

waters.name: Arkansas River
waters.note: Gold Medal water. The caddis hatch works upstream from Cañon City through May.

waters.name: Blue River
waters.note: Tailwater below Dillon, running through Silverthorne. Technical, mysis-fed, and open all winter.

seasons.what: Tailwaters only. Midges, then the first Baetis on warmer afternoons.
Blue-wing olives, then the Arkansas caddis hatch climbing upstream. Freestone runoff begins.
Peak snowmelt. Most freestone rivers are off; fish tailwaters, and the high lakes as they thaw.
Green drakes on the Fryingpan and Roaring Fork, PMDs, terrestrials, and the high country finally open.
Baetis, pre-spawn browns and the best few weeks of the year.
Back to midges and small nymphs on the tailwaters.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 16. Anglers 18 to 64 must also buy one Habitat Stamp per license year.
The annual license year runs 1 March to 31 March of the following year — thirteen months.
Many tailwaters are catch-and-release, artificial flies and lures only, including Cheesman Canyon and much of the Fryingpan.
Fishing two rods at once requires a Second Rod Stamp.
Greenback cutthroat recovery streams carry their own rules and some are closed outright. Check the water before you fish it.

license.priceNote: Figures are CPW's 2026 published rates for an adult annual fishing license. A Habitat Stamp, $12.76 for residents and non-residents alike, is required in addition for anglers 18 to 64. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Michigan
answer: Michigan fly fishing is spring-fed sand and gravel river fishing, with wild brook, brown and rainbow trout, plus Great Lakes steelhead running the same rivers. The Au Sable, Manistee, Pere Marquette and Muskegon are the headline waters. One all-species license covers everything, inland trout season opens the last Saturday in April, and the Hex hatch in late June is fished after dark.
summary: Spring-fed rivers, wild brook trout and night fishing. The Au Sable's Holy Water, the Hex hatch in June, and steelhead on the Pere Marquette.
whatMakesItDifferent: Michigan's trout rivers run on groundwater through sand and gravel, so flows and temperatures stay steady and there is no snowmelt blowout to plan around — the season runs on a calendar rather than on the weather. Two things follow from that. The first is the Hex hatch: Hexagenia limbata is a very large burrowing mayfly that emerges after dark in late June and early July on the Au Sable and Manistee, and the whole fishery reorganises around casting blind, in the dark, at the sound of a rising fish. The second is that these rivers are open to the Great Lakes, so the same water that holds resident wild brown trout in June holds steelhead out of Lake Michigan or Lake Huron in November. Michigan also has a good claim on American fly fishing's most-used dry fly: the Adams was tied in Mayfield, Michigan in 1922 by Len Halladay for a visiting angler, Charles Adams, who fished it on the Boardman.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: The state fish and the only native trout. Wild populations are strongest in the Upper Peninsula.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and often large. Brown trout were first planted in United States waters in a Pere Marquette tributary in 1884.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Resident stream fish, and the same species as the lake-run steelhead.

species.name: Steelhead
species.note: Autumn and spring runs out of Lake Michigan and Lake Huron.

species.name: Chinook and coho salmon
species.note: Autumn runs. Big fish, and not always interested in a fly.

waters.name: Au Sable River
waters.note: The Holy Water, from Burton's Landing to Wakeley Bridge, is flies only and catch and release.

waters.name: Manistee River
waters.note: A heavy Hex hatch and a serious night fishery; the lower river gets steelhead.

waters.name: Pere Marquette River
waters.note: A flies-only catch-and-release section upstream, and the best-known steelhead water in the state below it.

waters.name: Muskegon River
waters.note: Tailwater below Croton Dam. Steelhead in season and good dry-fly water in summer.

waters.name: Boardman River
waters.note: Near Traverse City, and where the Adams was first fished.

waters.name: Upper Peninsula streams
waters.note: Small, cedar-lined wild brook trout water — the Fox and the Escanaba among them.

seasons.what: Inland trout season opens the last Saturday in April — 25 April in 2026. Black stoneflies and the first Hendricksons.
Hendricksons, then sulphurs and caddis. The best daytime dry-fly fishing of the year.
The Hex hatch, after dark. Big flies, big fish, and a lot of standing still in the dark.
Tricos and terrestrials in the morning, and mousing after dark for brown trout.
Salmon first, then steelhead on the Pere Marquette, Muskegon and Manistee.
Year-round gear-restricted sections stay open, and the bigger rivers hold winter steelhead.

regulations: One all-species fishing license covers trout and salmon — there is no separate trout stamp. Everyone 17 and older needs one.
The statewide inland trout season opens the last Saturday in April, with a long list of year-round and gear-restricted exceptions.
The Au Sable Holy Water and the Pere Marquette flies-only water are artificial flies only and catch and release.
Trout rules are set stretch by stretch under a stream type system. The DNR's inland trout and salmon regulations map is the quickest way to check a specific piece of water before you fish it.

license.priceNote: Figures are the DNR's 2026 rates for an annual all-species fishing license, each including a $1 surcharge. The 2026 license is valid through 31 March 2027. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Wyoming
answer: Wyoming fly fishing is big-water tailwater and freestone fishing at altitude, with rainbow, brown, brook and several cutthroat as the mainstays. The North Platte, Snake, Green and the park waters are the headline rivers. A license is required from age 14, and an annual license also needs a Conservation Stamp. June through September is the heart of the season.
summary: Tailwater rainbows on the North Platte, native fine-spotted cutthroat on the Snake, and park water that needs its own permit. Hopper fishing in August.
whatMakesItDifferent: Wyoming holds two kinds of trout fishing that have very little to do with each other. The North Platte below Gray Reef is a dam-fed tailwater carrying an enormous head of heavy rainbows that eat scuds, leeches and midges all winter, and it fishes when most of the Rockies is frozen. An afternoon west, the Snake around Jackson is a freestone river holding Snake River fine-spotted cutthroat — a trout found in this drainage and almost nowhere else — which rise to a big foam dry with none of the suspicion a tailwater fish shows. Then there is the complication every visitor runs into: a large share of Wyoming's famous water lies inside Yellowstone National Park, which sells its own permit and does not accept the state license. Plan the park as a separate trip with separate paperwork.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: The North Platte tailwaters hold them in numbers and in size.

species.name: Snake River fine-spotted cutthroat
species.note: Native to the Snake drainage and effectively nowhere else. Freely rises to a dry fly.

species.name: Yellowstone cutthroat
species.note: Native to the Yellowstone and upper Shoshone drainages.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Strongest on the North Platte and the Green, and hard to move in daylight.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Small mountain streams and beaver ponds across the ranges.

species.name: Golden trout
species.note: High lakes in the Wind River Range. A long walk, and the reason people make it.

species.name: Mountain whitefish
species.note: Native and abundant, and a reliable winter fish.

waters.name: North Platte — Gray Reef
waters.note: Tailwater below the dam. Scuds, leeches and midges, and trout heavier than the river looks like it should hold.

waters.name: North Platte — Miracle Mile
waters.note: The stretch between Kortes and Pathfinder. Open, windy, and worth it in autumn.

waters.name: Snake River
waters.note: Around Jackson. Fine-spotted cutthroat on big dries, with the Tetons for scenery.

waters.name: Green River
waters.note: Below Fontenelle. Big water, big browns, and a strong terrestrial season.

waters.name: Yellowstone National Park waters
waters.note: The Firehole, Madison and Lamar. A park permit is required; a Wyoming license is not valid.

waters.name: Wind River Range lakes
waters.note: Backcountry stillwater for golden and cutthroat trout. A multi-day walk.

seasons.what: Tailwater fishing. Midges and scuds on the North Platte while the freestone rivers sit under ice.
Baetis on the tailwaters, then runoff begins. The Platte stays fishable when the Snake does not.
Peak snowmelt on the freestone rivers. Salmonflies and golden stones once the water starts to drop.
Terrestrial season. Hoppers, ants and beetles on the Snake and the Green, and the high lakes finally thaw.
Baetis, aggressive pre-spawn browns, and the Miracle Mile at its best. Then back to midges.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 14. An annual license must be bought with a Conservation Stamp, which is valid twelve months and covers hunting and fishing both; daily licenses do not need one.
Yellowstone National Park sells its own fishing permit and a Wyoming license is not valid inside the park. The park's rules, seasons and tackle restrictions are its own.
Wyoming has no general stream access right of the kind Montana has. The water may be public while the bed beneath it is not — float through, and get permission before you wade private ground.
Many waters carry their own creel, season and tackle rules, and they change annually. Check the regulations for the stretch you intend to fish.

license.priceNote: Wyoming sells fishing in two parts. The resident total is a $27 twelve-month fishing license plus the $21.50 Conservation Stamp; the non-resident total is $102 plus the same $21.50 stamp. The stamp is valid twelve months from purchase and covers hunting as well. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Utah
answer: Utah fly fishing is tailwater and mountain lake fishing in desert country, with rainbow, brown and brook trout, three native cutthroat subspecies and a well-known tiger trout fishery. The Green, Provo and Weber are the headline rivers. A license is required from age 12, and most waters are open all year.
summary: The Green below Flaming Gorge, clear enough to count fish from the trail. Technical tailwaters on the Provo, and tiger trout in the mountain lakes.
whatMakesItDifferent: The Green River below Flaming Gorge is the reason people fly to Utah. Water released from the bottom of the reservoir runs cold and startlingly clear all year, and the stretch below the dam carries one of the densest trout populations in the United States — clear enough that the trail along the canyon rim is a viewing platform, and you can choose a fish before you cast to it. That visibility cuts both ways: these trout see the angler as plainly as the angler sees them, and long leaders and small flies are not optional. Utah's second quirk is its stillwater. The mountain lakes on Boulder Mountain and the Uintas are stocked with tiger trout, a sterile brown-brook hybrid that grows fast and takes a fly hard, and they have turned alpine lake fishing from a curiosity into a reason to plan a trip.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Widespread, and the backbone of the Green and the Provo.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and large on the Green and the lower Provo.

species.name: Bonneville cutthroat
species.note: Native to the Bonneville basin, and the state fish.

species.name: Colorado River cutthroat
species.note: Native in the eastern drainages.

species.name: Yellowstone cutthroat
species.note: Native in the Bear River drainage in the north.

species.name: Tiger trout
species.note: A sterile brown-brook hybrid stocked in mountain lakes. Aggressive, and grows quickly.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: High streams and lakes across the Uintas and Boulder Mountain.

waters.name: Green River — A section
waters.note: Below Flaming Gorge. Extraordinary trout numbers in water clear enough to sight fish from above.

waters.name: Middle Provo River
waters.note: Restored meanders between Jordanelle and Deer Creek. Even flows and a dependable hatch calendar.

waters.name: Lower Provo River
waters.note: Below Deer Creek, running into Provo Canyon. Heavier browns and more pressure.

waters.name: Weber River
waters.note: Less famous than the Provo and often less crowded, with good brown trout water.

waters.name: Logan River
waters.note: Northern canyon water holding native Bonneville cutthroat.

waters.name: Boulder Mountain lakes
waters.note: A high plateau of small lakes for tiger, brook and cutthroat trout.

seasons.what: The Green and the Provo fish all winter. Midges, small Baetis, and very few people.
Blue-wing olives, then the cicadas on the Green in late May — the busiest and best-known weeks of the year.
Runoff on the freestone water. Tailwaters carry the month, and the high lakes begin to open.
PMDs, terrestrials, and the mountain lakes at their best. Fish the canyon water early in the heat.
Baetis, pre-spawn browns, and streamer fishing. The tailwaters never close.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 12. Most Utah waters are open to fishing year-round, with exceptions listed in the guidebook.
Fishing with two poles at once requires a separate two-pole permit.
Blue Ribbon and other special-regulation waters carry their own tackle and harvest rules — much of the Green and stretches of the Provo among them.
Rules are set water by water in the annual fishing guidebook, and they change. Check the stretch before you fish it.

license.priceNote: Figures are the DWR's 2026 rates for an adult 365-day fishing license, ages 18 to 64. Non-resident fees rose from $94 to $120 on 1 July 2025. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Oregon
answer: Oregon fly fishing runs from spring-fed trout rivers to summer steelhead on big western water, with wild redband and rainbow trout, cutthroat, brown trout and sea-run steelhead. The Deschutes, Metolius, McKenzie and North Umpqua are the headline rivers. A license is required from age 12, and steelhead and salmon need extra tags.
summary: Summer steelhead on the Deschutes and North Umpqua, spring-fed redbands on the Metolius, and the river where the drift boat was invented.
whatMakesItDifferent: Oregon is where a trout angler has to decide whether to become a steelhead angler. The lower Deschutes and the North Umpqua hold summer-run steelhead that will come up through several feet of water for a swung fly, and the whole culture around them — two-handed rods, a greased line, first light, long fishless days — is a different sport from matching a hatch. The state then gives you the opposite extreme in the Metolius, which emerges from the ground near Camp Sherman at a near-constant temperature and runs so cold and clear through the pines that its wild redbands are considered some of the most difficult trout in the West. A rule worth knowing before you book: on the lower Deschutes you may float a boat, but you may not fish from one. You get out and wade.

species.name: Redband trout
species.note: The native interior rainbow. The Deschutes and Metolius fish are wild and hard-fighting.

species.name: Summer steelhead
species.note: Deschutes and North Umpqua runs, from roughly July into the autumn.

species.name: Winter steelhead
species.note: Coastal rivers, from late autumn into spring.

species.name: Coastal cutthroat
species.note: Small coastal streams and the lower reaches of the bigger rivers.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Widespread, and the main quarry on the McKenzie and the Williamson.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The Williamson and the Wood, where they reach serious size.

species.name: Bull trout
species.note: Native char, strongest in the Metolius. Protected — check the rules before targeting them.

waters.name: Lower Deschutes River
waters.note: Salmonflies in May, summer steelhead from July. You may float it, but you must fish from the bank.

waters.name: North Umpqua
waters.note: A long fly-only stretch of summer steelhead water, and some of the hardest wading in the state.

waters.name: Metolius River
waters.note: Spring-fed, gin-clear and cold year-round. Wild redbands with a reputation for refusing everything.

waters.name: McKenzie River
waters.note: Where the McKenzie drift boat was developed. Green drakes in early summer.

waters.name: Williamson River
waters.note: Big Klamath-basin redbands that run up out of the lake in summer.

waters.name: Rogue River
waters.note: Half-pounder steelhead in autumn — small, numerous and a good first swung-fly fish.

seasons.what: Winter steelhead on the coastal rivers. Blue-wing olives on the Deschutes on grey afternoons.
The Deschutes salmonfly hatch, usually mid to late May. The best dry-fly weeks of the year.
Green drakes on the McKenzie, caddis everywhere, and the high country starting to open.
Summer steelhead on the Deschutes and North Umpqua. Early and late; the middle of the day is for sleeping.
Half-pounders on the Rogue, Baetis on the trout rivers, and the first winter fish on the coast.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 12. Targeting salmon, steelhead or sturgeon also needs a Combined Angling Tag.
A Columbia River Basin Endorsement is required to fish for salmon, steelhead or sturgeon in the Columbia and its tributaries — the Deschutes among them.
Wild fish are identified by an intact adipose fin. Hatchery fish are fin-clipped, and harvest rules turn on that difference.
On the lower Deschutes you may not angle from a floating device. Float to the water, then get out and wade.
Regulations are set zone by zone and change in-season. Check the current rules and any emergency closures before you go.

license.agency: Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife
license.priceNote: Figures are ODFW's 2026 rates for an annual angling license and include the agent fee. Fees rose in 2026 for the first time since 2020 — the resident licence was $44 and the non-resident $110.50. Salmon, steelhead and sturgeon need a Combined Angling Tag on top. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: New York
answer: New York fly fishing is Catskill and Adirondack river fishing with a long history, holding wild brown and rainbow trout, native brook trout, and Great Lakes steelhead in the tributaries. The Beaverkill, Willowemoc and Upper Delaware are the headline waters. A license is required from age 16, and most trout streams are catch and release outside the April to October season.
summary: Where American dry-fly fishing started. The Beaverkill and Willowemoc, the wild and difficult Upper Delaware, and Adirondack pocket water.
whatMakesItDifferent: The Catskills are the birthplace of American dry-fly fishing, and that is a matter of record rather than marketing. Theodore Gordon was tying and fishing upright-winged duns on the Neversink in the 1890s, the Catskill style of tying came out of these valleys, and the Junction Pool at Roscoe — where the Willowemoc meets the Beaverkill — is the most photographed confluence in American angling. Two hours west the Upper Delaware is a different proposition entirely: its flows are governed by releases from New York City's water-supply reservoirs under an interstate agreement, so the river runs cold through a Pennsylvania-latitude summer and holds wild, large and famously selective browns and rainbows. Nobody describes the Delaware as easy. Then, in the Adirondacks, the West Branch of the Ausable is pure pocket water — boulders, seams and short drifts, fished on foot.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and self-sustaining on the Delaware system and much of the Catskills.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Wild in the Upper Delaware, where they run large and spook easily.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: The state fish and the only native trout. Adirondack streams and ponds.

species.name: Steelhead
species.note: Lake Ontario tributaries, chiefly the Salmon River, from autumn into spring.

species.name: Landlocked Atlantic salmon
species.note: A handful of Adirondack waters and some Lake Ontario tributaries.

waters.name: Beaverkill River
waters.note: The most storied trout stream in the country, and still a genuinely good one.

waters.name: Willowemoc Creek
waters.note: Meets the Beaverkill at Junction Pool in Roscoe. Smaller, and often kinder.

waters.name: West Branch Delaware
waters.note: Cold reservoir releases, wild browns and rainbows, and fish that refuse for a living.

waters.name: Esopus Creek
waters.note: Catskill freestone fed by the Shandaken tunnel, which keeps it cool in summer.

waters.name: West Branch Ausable
waters.note: Adirondack pocket water — boulders, seams and short, accurate drifts.

waters.name: Salmon River
waters.note: Pulaski. Lake Ontario steelhead and salmon, and crowds to match in the best weeks.

seasons.what: Catch-and-release season on most trout streams. Midges, and steelhead on the Salmon River.
The harvest season opens 1 April. Hendricksons and blue quills as the water warms.
March browns, sulphurs, then the Delaware green drake and coffin fly. The best weeks of the year.
Tricos at dawn and terrestrials through the day. The tailwaters hold up when the freestone streams get warm.
Baetis and isonychia, then steelhead moving into the Lake Ontario tributaries.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 16. A licence is valid for 365 days from the date you buy it, not to a fixed calendar date.
Under the statewide trout stream regulations, most streams run an April to mid-October season for harvest, and are catch and release with artificial lures only for the rest of the year.
Trout streams are assigned management categories — wild, wild-quality, stocked and stocked-extended — and the category sets the rules for that stretch.
Saltwater fishing needs a free marine registration instead of a licence.
Rules differ stream by stream and change. Check the stretch you intend to fish before you go.

license.agency: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
license.priceNote: Figures are DEC's published rates for an annual freshwater fishing licence, residents aged 16 to 69. Residents 70 and over pay $5. The licence runs 365 days from purchase. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: North Carolina
answer: North Carolina fly fishing is small-stream Appalachian fishing, with native Southern Appalachian brook trout in the headwaters and wild and stocked brown and rainbow trout below them. The Davidson, Nantahala, Tuckasegee and the Smokies streams are the headline waters. A license is required from age 16, and the inland licence covers mountain trout water with no separate stamp.
summary: Native brook trout in headwater streams, technical browns on the Davidson, and delayed-harvest water that fishes beautifully from October to June.
whatMakesItDifferent: North Carolina classifies every piece of trout water and regulates it by class, and once that clicks the whole state makes sense. Hatchery Supported water is stocked and closes for a month before the spring opening. Wild Trout water is self-sustaining, artificial lures only, and usually small. Catch and Release water is exactly that. And Delayed Harvest — a Southeastern invention — is stocked heavily and run as artificial-lures-only catch and release from October until the first Saturday in June, which turns ordinary streams into excellent fly water through the months when most of the country has stopped fishing. Above all of it sit the native Southern Appalachian brook trout, the 'specks', holding on in cold headwater streams above the places rainbows and browns took over a century ago. They are small, they are beautiful, and reaching them involves more walking than casting.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Southern Appalachian strain, the only native trout, in high cold headwaters. Locally called specks.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild in many mountain streams, and the largest fish in the state.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Wild in much of the mountain water and stocked in the rest.

species.name: Smallmouth bass
species.note: The warmer valley rivers, and a good hot-weather alternative to trout.

waters.name: Davidson River
waters.note: In Pisgah National Forest. Well-fed, well-educated trout below the hatchery and a reputation for humbling people.

waters.name: Nantahala River
waters.note: Delayed-harvest water, cold all summer from the dam release above it.

waters.name: Tuckasegee River
waters.note: Big, accessible delayed-harvest water near Sylva — the easiest good trout river in the state to wade.

waters.name: Wilson Creek
waters.note: A wild and scenic river in the Grandfather district. Wild trout and real gradient.

waters.name: Great Smoky Mountains streams
waters.note: Deep Creek, Oconaluftee and Hazel Creek. Park rules apply, and a NC or Tennessee licence is valid.

waters.name: South Toe River
waters.note: Below Mount Mitchell. Cold, small and good brook trout country upstream.

seasons.what: Delayed-harvest water opens 1 October and fishes at its best straight away. Browns colour up and get territorial.
Nymphs, midges and the occasional blue-wing olive. The delayed-harvest rivers stay open and stay quiet.
Hatchery Supported water closes ahead of the spring opening. Wild and delayed-harvest water stays open — and hatches start.
The spring opening on Hatchery Supported water, Quill Gordons, March browns and caddis. The high country wakes up.
Terrestrials and small dries on the headwater brook trout streams. Fish high, where the water stays cold.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 16. The annual inland fishing licence includes Public Mountain Trout Waters and trout waters on game lands — there is no separate trout stamp to buy on top of it.

Trout water is regulated by class: Hatchery Supported, Wild Trout, Catch and Release, and Delayed Harvest. Each class has its own season, tackle rules and limits, and the signs at the access point tell you which one you are on.
Delayed Harvest water is artificial lures only and catch and release from 1 October until the first Saturday in June.
Hatchery Supported water closes from 1 March until 7am on the first Saturday in April.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park has its own rules. A North Carolina or Tennessee fishing licence is valid inside it, and no trout stamp is needed.

license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026 published rates for an annual State Inland Fishing licence, which includes Public Mountain Trout Waters. It does not cover coastal waters, which need a separate licence. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: California
answer: California fly fishing runs from Sierra freestone and spring creeks to big valley tailwaters, with rainbow, brown and brook trout, native golden trout in the high country and wild redbands in the north. The Lower Sacramento, Hat Creek, Fall River, Owens and Upper Sacramento are the headline waters. A license is required from age 16, and seasons vary water by water.
summary: Spring creeks at Hat Creek and Fall River, big tailwater rainbows on the Lower Sacramento, and golden trout in the High Sierra.
whatMakesItDifferent: Almost every hatchery rainbow trout on earth traces back to California. Eggs taken from the McCloud River in the 1870s and 1880s were shipped east and then worldwide, and the rainbow trout now swimming in New Zealand, Patagonia and most of Europe descend from that stock. The state also invented the idea of managing a river for wild fish rather than for stocking: Hat Creek became California's first designated wild trout water in 1971, and the programme that followed is why the spring creeks around Fall River Mills still fish the way they do. Set against that, the practical reality of fishing here is altitude and distance. Golden trout, the state fish, live above 10,000 feet in the Sierra and take a serious walk to reach, while the Lower Sacramento runs through farmland at 300 feet and fishes from a boat. The two have nothing in common except the licence.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Everywhere, and the Lower Sacramento fish are heavy and hard-running.

species.name: Golden trout
species.note: The state fish. Native to the Kern drainage and planted in High Sierra lakes above 10,000 feet.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The Owens, the East Walker and the Truckee hold the biggest of them.

species.name: Redband trout
species.note: Native in the McCloud and the far north.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Sierra lakes and small streams, abundant and willing.

species.name: Lahontan cutthroat
species.note: Native to the eastern Sierra drainages, restored in a handful of waters.

species.name: Steelhead
species.note: Coastal rivers in winter, under tight and frequently changing rules.

waters.name: Lower Sacramento River
waters.note: Big tailwater below Redding. Heavy rainbows, mostly fished from a drift boat.

waters.name: Hat Creek
waters.note: California's first wild trout water. Flat, clear spring-creek fishing that rewards a long leader.

waters.name: Fall River
waters.note: Spring-fed and mostly fished from a boat, because wading ruins it. Famously technical.

waters.name: Owens River
waters.note: Eastern Sierra. The Upper Owens, the gorge and the wild trout section all fish differently.

waters.name: Upper Sacramento
waters.note: Freestone water along the I-5 corridor near Dunsmuir. Accessible and generous.

waters.name: Golden Trout Wilderness
waters.note: High Sierra headwaters for native golden trout. Days of walking, small fish, and worth it.

seasons.what: Tailwaters and the year-round sections. Baetis on the Lower Sacramento, midges elsewhere.
The general trout opener on many Sierra waters, usually the last Saturday in April. Caddis and the first mayflies.
Snowmelt in the Sierra. The valley tailwaters and the spring creeks carry the month.
PMDs, tricos and terrestrials. The high country opens up and the goldens become reachable.
The best weeks on the Lower Sacramento and the Owens, then winter steelhead on the coast.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 16. A licence runs 365 days from the date you buy it.
Seasons differ by water. Many Sierra waters run from the last Saturday in April to 15 November, while a number of rivers and all the big tailwaters are open year-round.
Wild Trout and Heritage Trout waters carry their own tackle and harvest rules, often artificial lures with barbless hooks.
Fishing two rods at once in fresh water needs a Second Rod Validation. Steelhead anglers need a Steelhead Report-Restoration Card.
Coastal steelhead rules change in-season and some rivers close at short notice. Check before you travel.

license.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife
license.priceNote: Figures are CDFW's 2026 rates for an annual sport fishing licence, ages 16 and over, and include the agent handling and application fees. Validations and report cards are extra. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Washington
answer: Washington fly fishing means one great year-round trout river, a lot of stillwater, and some of the best winter steelhead country left in the lower 48. The Yakima, the Olympic Peninsula rivers and the desert seepage lakes are the headline waters. A license is required from age 15, and steelhead and salmon rules change in-season.
summary: The Yakima as the state's one true trout river, Olympic Peninsula winter steelhead, and desert lakes holding rainbows that behave like saltwater fish.
whatMakesItDifferent: Washington is not a trout state in the way Montana is, and pretending otherwise leads visitors to the wrong water. It has essentially one major year-round trout river — the Yakima, which runs through sagebrush canyon east of the Cascades and fishes on a proper hatch calendar. What the state has instead is the rainforest rivers of the Olympic Peninsula, where wild winter steelhead come in from the Pacific between December and April, and a network of desert seepage lakes in the Columbia Basin where rainbows feed on scuds and damselflies and grow faster than any river fish. The thing to understand before booking anything is that Washington manages wild steelhead by closing water. Rivers open and shut in-season by emergency rule, sometimes within days, so a trip planned around a specific river needs checking the week you leave and again the morning you go.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: The Yakima's wild rainbows, and the fast-growing fish of the desert lakes.

species.name: Westslope cutthroat
species.note: Native in the upper Yakima and across the eastern streams.

species.name: Coastal cutthroat
species.note: Sea-run fish in the lowland rivers and Puget Sound beaches.

species.name: Winter steelhead
species.note: Olympic Peninsula rivers from December into April. Wild, and tightly protected.

species.name: Summer steelhead
species.note: Columbia tributaries including the Methow and the Grande Ronde.

species.name: Bull trout
species.note: Native char, protected. Learn to tell them from a rainbow before you fish the upper rivers.

waters.name: Yakima River
waters.note: The state's one genuine year-round trout river. Canyon water, wild rainbows and cutthroat.

waters.name: Hoh, Sol Duc and Bogachiel
waters.note: Olympic Peninsula rainforest rivers. Wild winter steelhead, heavy rain, short days.

waters.name: Skagit River
waters.note: Big water with a managed catch-and-release steelhead season when returns allow it.

waters.name: Methow River
waters.note: Eastern Cascades. Summer steelhead and good trout water above them.

waters.name: Rocky Ford Creek
waters.note: A spring creek in the desert. No wading, big rainbows, and a hard lesson in drag.

waters.name: Lenice and Nunnally Lakes
waters.note: Columbia Basin seepage lakes. Fly-only, barbless, and rainbows that run.

seasons.what: Olympic Peninsula winter steelhead. Watch the closures, and bring more rain gear than you think.
The desert lakes come alive — chironomids first, then damsels. Skwalas on the Yakima in March.
PMDs and caddis on the Yakima. Mountain streams open as the snow goes.
Terrestrial season on the Yakima, and summer steelhead on the Methow and Grande Ronde.
October caddis, Baetis, and the first winter fish reaching the coast.

regulations: A fishing license is required from age 15. The annual freshwater licence includes a Vehicle Access Pass for WDFW land; other state land needs a separate Discover Pass.
Salmon and steelhead anglers need a catch record card, and from 1 January 2026 a Columbia River Salmon and Steelhead Endorsement to fish for them in the Columbia and many of its tributaries.
Wild steelhead are release-only across most of the state, and whole rivers close in-season by emergency rule. Check the emergency rules the week you travel.
Many waters are selective gear rules: no bait, single barbless hooks, and in some cases no fishing from a boat.
Rules are set water by water in the sport fishing pamphlet and change frequently.

license.agency: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife
license.priceNote: Figures are WDFW's rates effective 1 January 2026 for an annual freshwater licence, ages 16 to 69, and include the Vehicle Access Pass. Licence fees rose about 38 per cent under 2025 legislation. The Columbia River endorsement is a further $8.75. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Wisconsin
answer: Wisconsin fly fishing is Driftless Area spring creek fishing, with wild brown trout in extraordinary numbers, native brook trout in the colder headwaters, and Lake Superior steelhead in the north. Timber Coulee, the West Fork of the Kickapoo and Black Earth Creek are the headline waters. You need a licence and an inland trout stamp, and the catch-and-release season starts in January.
summary: Driftless Area spring creeks with some of the highest wild brown trout densities in the country, and thousands of acres of easement access.
whatMakesItDifferent: The Driftless Area is the part of the upper Midwest the last glaciers missed. No ice sheet flattened it, so instead of the lake-and-bog country around it you get steep wooded coulees, limestone bedrock and hundreds of cold spring creeks running through farmland. Some of those creeks hold wild brown trout at densities that rival anywhere in the United States — thousands of fish per mile in the best stretches — and they are small enough to cross in two strides. The second thing that makes this work is unglamorous and more important: decades of habitat restoration paid for by trout stamps, and a state easement programme that bought public fishing rights across private farmland. You park at a sign, climb a stile and fish, on water somebody else owns. Very few states have made small-stream trout fishing this available to people who do not own land.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and self-sustaining throughout the Driftless, and the main quarry.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native, and strongest in the coldest headwaters and the northern counties.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Less common inland; the Lake Superior tributaries hold the migratory ones.

species.name: Steelhead
species.note: Lake Superior and Lake Michigan tributaries, chiefly the Bois Brule.

waters.name: Timber Coulee Creek
waters.note: Near Coon Valley. The restoration project that proved the whole Driftless model works.

waters.name: West Fork Kickapoo River
waters.note: Vernon County. Easement access, wild browns and a long season.

waters.name: Black Earth Creek
waters.note: Half an hour from Madison, and far better than a creek that close to a city ought to be.

waters.name: Castle Rock Creek
waters.note: Grant County spring creek, fertile and open, with sight-fishing in low water.

waters.name: Bois Brule River
waters.note: Northern Wisconsin. Steelhead, big browns and a long presidential history.

waters.name: Namekagon River
waters.note: A National Scenic Riverway holding wild browns and brook trout.

seasons.what: The early catch-and-release season. Midges and small nymphs on spring creeks that never freeze.
The general season opens the first Saturday. Caddis, Hendricksons and sulphurs — the best hatches of the year.
Sulphurs into the evening, and the first good terrestrial fishing as the hay gets cut.
Hopper season. Low clear water, long leaders and short casts to the undercut banks.
Tricos, Baetis and pre-spawn browns to the close of the general season on 15 October.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 16, and an inland trout stamp is required in addition to fish for trout on inland waters.
The early season runs from 1 January to the Friday before the general opener: catch and release, artificial lures only.
The general inland trout season runs from the first Saturday in May to 15 October.
A Great Lakes trout and salmon stamp is a separate purchase from the inland trout stamp, for the Lake Michigan and Lake Superior tributaries.
Streams are classified and regulated individually, and easement access is marked by yellow signs. Respect the crops and the fences.

license.priceNote: Wisconsin sells trout fishing in two parts. The resident total is a $20 annual fishing licence plus the $10 inland trout stamp; the non-resident total is $55 plus the same $10 stamp. The licence year starts 1 April. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Arkansas
answer: Arkansas fly fishing is tailwater fishing below deep Ozark reservoirs, with rainbow, brown, brook and cutthroat trout in water far too cold for the latitude. The White River, the Norfork and the Little Red are the headline waters. You need a licence and a trout permit, the fishing is good all year, and the dam release schedule decides your day.
summary: World-class brown trout in Ozark tailwaters, fishable twelve months a year — if you read the generation schedule before you drive out.
whatMakesItDifferent: Arkansas should not have trout at all. It sits at the latitude of Memphis, and before the dams its rivers ran warm. Then the Corps of Engineers built Bull Shoals, Norfork and Greers Ferry, and the water they release comes off the bottom of very deep reservoirs at around fifty degrees all year. The result is several hundred miles of cold river in the Ozarks, holding brown trout as large as any in North America — the Little Red River produced a world-record brown of 40 pounds 4 ounces in 1992. The catch is that the river is a machine with a switch. When the dam generates, the flow can rise several feet in under an hour and wading water becomes a boat river. Checking the generation schedule before you drive out is not a refinement here; it is the difference between a day's fishing and standing on a gravel bar watching the river come up.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The reason people come. The White and the Little Red grow them to extraordinary size.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Stocked heavily and abundant throughout the tailwaters.

species.name: Cutthroat trout
species.note: Stocked in the White and the Norfork, and a genuine novelty this far east.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: A small stocked population in the Norfork tailwater.

species.name: Smallmouth bass
species.note: The warmer Ozark streams above the dams — Crooked Creek and the Buffalo.

waters.name: White River
waters.note: Below Bull Shoals. A hundred miles of cold water and the state's signature trout fishery.

waters.name: North Fork River
waters.note: The Norfork tailwater. Short, rich and heavily fished, with a catch-and-release section.

waters.name: Little Red River
waters.note: Below Greers Ferry. Where the 40-pound world-record brown came from in 1992.

waters.name: Spring River
waters.note: Fed by Mammoth Spring rather than a dam, so it runs cold without a generation schedule.

waters.name: Beaver Tailwater
waters.note: Below Beaver Lake. Smaller water, and quieter than the White.

waters.name: Buffalo National River
waters.note: Not trout water, but the best smallmouth river in the Ozarks and worth a day.

seasons.what: Low generation and good wading. Sow bugs, midges and streamers for post-spawn browns.
Caddis, and the heaviest generation of the year as the reservoirs shed spring rain. Fish from a boat.
Generation is usually heavy in the afternoon for power demand. Fish early, or fish from a boat.
Flows settle. Terrestrials, hopper-dropper and the best wading of the year.
Brown trout spawn. Big fish move, and the spawning shoals carry restrictions — stay off the redds.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 16, and a trout permit is required in addition to fish the tailwaters or keep a trout.
The trout permit applies on the tailwaters below Beaver, Bull Shoals, Norfork, Greers Ferry and Lake Greeson — which is to say, on all the water this page is about.
Stretches of the White and the Norfork are catch and release with artificial lures only, and the boundaries are signed.
Dam generation is scheduled by the Southwestern Power Administration, not by the Game and Fish Commission. Check the release schedule before you travel and again before you wade.
Seasonal restrictions protect spawning brown trout in autumn and winter. Check the current rules.

license.priceNote: Arkansas sells trout fishing in two parts. The resident total is a $10.50 Fisheries Conservation Licence plus the $10 resident trout permit; the non-resident total is a $60 annual licence plus the $20 non-resident trout permit. Resident licences run to 30 June. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: New Mexico
answer: New Mexico fly fishing is high-desert tailwater and canyon fishing, with rainbow and brown trout, native Rio Grande cutthroat and the rare Gila trout. The San Juan below Navajo Dam is the headline water, with the Rio Grande gorge, the Cimarron and the Pecos behind it. A license is required from age 12, and the San Juan fishes every month of the year.
summary: The San Juan Quality Waters below Navajo Dam — tiny flies, enormous rainbows, twelve months a year — plus two of the rarest trout in America.
whatMakesItDifferent: Four miles of river carry New Mexico's reputation. The Quality Waters of the San Juan, immediately below Navajo Dam, hold rainbow trout in densities and sizes that make no sense in a desert at 5,700 feet, fed by cold reservoir releases and an inexhaustible supply of midges. The fishing there is a discipline of its own: size 22 to 26 flies, 6X and 7X tippet, and trout that have seen more anglers than almost any fish in the country. People fly in from everywhere, and they fish it in January. The rest of the state pulls in the opposite direction. The Rio Grande runs through a basalt gorge you climb down into, the Cimarron is a small canyon stream you can cross anywhere, and in the remote southwest the Gila trout — one of the rarest trout in North America, brought back from the edge of extinction — is fishable in a small number of waters under its own rules.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: The San Juan fish are the famous ones, and they are famously well-educated.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The Rio Grande, the Chama and the Cimarron, and bigger than the streams suggest.

species.name: Rio Grande cutthroat
species.note: The state fish and the southernmost cutthroat in the world. Remote headwater streams.

species.name: Gila trout
species.note: Native to the southwest, recovered from near-extinction, and fishable in a few waters under special rules.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: High-country streams and small lakes in the north.

waters.name: San Juan River — Quality Waters
waters.note: Below Navajo Dam. Midges, tiny tippet and very large rainbows, every month of the year.

waters.name: Rio Grande del Norte
waters.note: The gorge below Taos. A steep climb in, brown trout and pike-free solitude.

waters.name: Cimarron River
waters.note: A small canyon stream below Eagle Nest, holding more and better trout than its size suggests.

waters.name: Pecos River
waters.note: Headwaters in the Sangre de Cristos. Easy access and a good first New Mexico river.

waters.name: Rio Chama
waters.note: Tailwater below El Vado and Abiquiu. Big browns in autumn.

waters.name: Gila headwaters
waters.note: Remote southwest streams holding native Gila trout under their own regulations.

seasons.what: The San Juan at its quietest and most technical. Midges, and Baetis as the days lengthen.
Blue-wing olives on the San Juan, and the freestone streams clearing ahead of the mountain snowmelt.
Runoff in the high country. The San Juan and the Chama carry the month.
Monsoon season — afternoon storms that can blow a canyon stream out in an hour. Fish mornings, and watch the sky.
The best weeks of the year. Baetis, pre-spawn browns, and cool clear water everywhere.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 12. Every angler aged 18 and over also needs a Habitat Management and Access Validation, bought once per licence year.
A $10 Habitat Stamp is required in addition on Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management land, which covers a great deal of the state's trout water.
The licence year runs 1 April to 31 March.
The San Juan Quality Waters are artificial flies and lures with barbless hooks, and the uppermost stretch is catch and release. Limits and boundaries are signed.
Gila trout waters are opened and closed individually and carry their own rules. Check before you go.

license.agency: New Mexico Department of Game and Fish
license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026–27 rates and include the mandatory $4 Habitat Management and Access Validation on top of the $35 resident and $90 non-resident annual licence. A further $10 Habitat Stamp is required to fish Forest Service or BLM land. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.
